heading: What made another war possible twenty years after the last one
body: The Second World War is often introduced as though it began in 1939, which makes almost everything about it hard to understand. It is better read as the second half of a European crisis that opened in 1914 and was never resolved, with a second and largely separate war in Asia that had been running since 1931 and was eventually folded into it. The settlement of 1919 is where most accounts start, and it deserves more care than the shorthand "the Treaty of Versailles was too harsh" allows. Germany lost territory, its army was capped at a hundred thousand men, it was assigned responsibility for the war's damages, and it was presented with a reparations bill it regarded as ruinous. What mattered was less the severity than the combination: harsh enough to enrage a large, populous, industrially intact country, not harsh enough to disable it, and never enforced with any consistency. Germany's economy was the strongest in Europe in 1914 and was still the strongest in 1930. A settlement that humiliates a great power without removing its capacity is the worst of both worlds, and contemporaries said so at the time. The Depression turned resentment into politics. German unemployment passed six million in the early 1930s, banks failed, and the moderate parties that had governed the Weimar Republic were squeezed between communists and Nazis. Hitler became Chancellor in January 1933 through a constitutional appointment engineered by conservative politicians who believed they could use and contain him, and within eighteen months the republic had been dismantled from inside. What followed was a decade of tests. The Rhineland was remilitarised in 1936 against the treaty, and nothing happened. Austria was annexed in 1938, and nothing happened. At Munich later that year Britain and France agreed to Czechoslovakia's dismemberment in exchange for a promise of no further demands, and six months later Germany took the rest of the country anyway. Appeasement is easy to condemn in hindsight and was not simply cowardice: Britain and France had lost a generation of young men twenty years earlier, were rearming from a low base, and were governed by people who genuinely believed another general war would end European civilisation. They were not wrong about the cost. They were wrong that it could be avoided by concession. The last piece was the Nazi–Soviet Pact of August 1939, an agreement between two regimes that regarded each other as mortal enemies, containing a secret protocol dividing Poland and the Baltic states between them. It removed the one thing that had constrained German planning — the prospect of a war on two fronts — and it stunned communists across Europe. A week later Germany invaded Poland; Britain and France, who had guaranteed Poland after Munich taught them what German promises were worth, declared war on 3 September. The Soviet Union invaded Poland from the east on 17 September, and the two powers met in the middle of a country that had ceased to exist.

heading: 1939 to 1941: how Germany won everything and then did not stop
body: Poland fell in five weeks, and the way it fell established the pattern. German doctrine concentrated armour, motorised infantry and close air support on narrow fronts to punch through and then race for the rear, breaking communications and encircling armies that were still intact but no longer able to act. The press called it Blitzkrieg. It was less a formal doctrine than a set of tactical preferences combined with excellent radio discipline and commanders trusted to improvise, and it worked spectacularly against opponents whose command systems were slower. Then came seven months in which the Western Front barely moved — the Phoney War — while Germany prepared. In April 1940 Denmark and Norway were taken. In May the offensive in the west began, and what happened next remains among the most startling military results in modern history. The French army was large, well equipped and widely considered the strongest in Europe. The German plan sent its armoured weight through the Ardennes, wooded hills the French had assessed as difficult for tanks and therefore lightly held, crossed the Meuse, and drove for the Channel. It cut the Allied armies in half in ten days. The British Expeditionary Force and substantial French forces were pushed back to Dunkirk, from which some 338,000 men were evacuated in nine days by a fleet of warships and small civilian craft, without their equipment. France signed an armistice on 22 June. Six weeks had removed the Western Front. Britain fought on alone, and the summer of 1940 turned on a battle for air superiority that Germany needed before any invasion could be attempted. The Battle of Britain was won by a narrow margin and by unglamorous things: radar stations feeding a centralised control system that put fighters in the right place, aircraft production that outpaced losses, and a German decision to switch from attacking airfields to bombing cities at the moment when the airfields were close to breaking. The Blitz that followed killed some 40,000 civilians without breaking anything strategic. Invasion was postponed indefinitely. By 1941 Germany dominated Europe from the Atlantic to the Vistula, and it did not stop. In April it overran Yugoslavia and Greece to secure the Balkans. On 22 June it invaded the Soviet Union with something over three million men on a front stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea — the largest invasion ever mounted. The reasons were ideological as much as strategic: living space in the east, the destruction of what the regime called Judeo-Bolshevism, and the grain and oil that Germany could not otherwise reach. It was the decision that lost the war, and it was taken while Britain remained undefeated, which is precisely the two-front situation the pact had been signed to avoid.

heading: The Eastern Front, where the war was mainly decided
body: Anyone whose picture of the war comes from English-language film will underweight the Eastern Front, and the scale is worth stating plainly. Roughly three-quarters of German army casualties were inflicted there. The Soviet Union lost around 27 million people, military and civilian together — something like one in seven of its pre-war population, against Britain's roughly one in two hundred. The war in the east was fought at a level of ferocity that had no counterpart in the west, because both regimes regarded it as a war of annihilation and conducted it accordingly. The German advance in 1941 was initially overwhelming. Entire Soviet armies were encircled; the Kiev pocket alone yielded over 600,000 prisoners, of whom the great majority died in captivity, most of them deliberately starved. But the advance did not end the war, and by December it had stalled in front of Moscow, in temperatures for which the German army had not equipped itself, at the end of supply lines running on a rail gauge that did not match. A Soviet counter-offensive drove them back. The strategy that had beaten France in six weeks had no answer to a country that could trade space for time and had moved over 1,500 factories east of the Urals as the front collapsed. The turn came at Stalingrad. A summer offensive in 1942 aimed at the Caucasus oil fields was diverted into a city on the Volga that mattered as much for its name as its position, and it became a months-long battle fought room by room. In November Soviet forces struck the weakly held Romanian and Hungarian flanks and closed a ring around the German Sixth Army. Hitler forbade a breakout. Some 91,000 men surrendered in February 1943; around 5,000 came home. It was the first destruction of an entire German field army and it was understood as decisive at the time. Kursk followed in July 1943, a German attempt to pinch out a salient that the Soviets knew about in advance and had fortified in depth. It became the largest armoured engagement of the war and ended German offensive capability in the east permanently. From then on the direction of the front was one way. Operation Bagration in summer 1944 destroyed Army Group Centre and, in scale of loss, exceeded Stalingrad — and in most Western accounts it goes unmentioned, because it happened three weeks after Normandy. Two things sustained the Soviet effort: an industrial relocation and mobilisation of extraordinary brutality and effectiveness, and Lend-Lease, through which the United States supplied trucks, locomotives, radios, aviation fuel and food in quantities that did not win the war but substantially raised the speed at which the Red Army could advance.

heading: The war at sea, and the war in the air
body: Britain's survival depended on the Atlantic, and the Battle of the Atlantic ran from the first day of the war to the last. German submarines attacked the convoys carrying food, fuel and munitions, hunting in coordinated groups directed by radio from shore. Their peak came in early 1943, when shipping losses briefly threatened to outrun construction. The reversal, within months, came from the accumulation of small advantages rather than any single weapon: escort carriers and very long-range aircraft closing the mid-Atlantic air gap, centimetric radar that could find a surfaced submarine at night, high-frequency direction-finding that located boats by their own radio traffic, and above all the reading of German naval Enigma traffic by the codebreakers at Bletchley Park, which allowed convoys to be routed around waiting submarine lines. In May 1943 the German navy lost 41 boats and withdrew from the North Atlantic. Of roughly 40,000 men who served in the U-boat arm, around three-quarters were killed — the highest loss rate of any substantial force in the war. Codebreaking deserves its own note, because it was concealed for thirty years afterwards and therefore missing from the first generation of histories. The Polish Cipher Bureau broke Enigma before the war and passed its work to Britain and France in 1939; Bletchley Park industrialised it, building machines to test settings at speed. The intelligence, codenamed Ultra, shaped the Atlantic, the Mediterranean and the deception plan for Normandy. It shortened the war, by estimates of a year or more, and it worked only because its existence was protected with a discipline that sometimes meant not acting on what it revealed. The strategic bombing campaign is the war's most contested aspect and should be presented as such. Britain, having found daylight precision bombing suicidally costly, turned to night area bombing of cities; the United States persisted with daylight raids at appalling loss until long-range fighter escort became available in 1944. The campaign killed several hundred thousand German civilians, and firestorms at Hamburg and Dresden killed tens of thousands in single nights. It did not break German morale, and German war production actually rose until late 1944 as industry dispersed. What it did achieve was indirect and real: it forced Germany to divert enormous resources to air defence — thousands of guns and their crews, and a fighter force pulled back from the fronts — and the 1944 campaign against synthetic oil plants left the Luftwaffe with aircraft and no fuel to fly them. Whether those results justified the means is a moral argument that has not been settled and should not be presented as though it has.

heading: The Pacific war, which was already running before 1939
body: The Pacific war did not begin at Pearl Harbor. Japan had seized Manchuria in 1931 and invaded China proper in 1937, and by 1941 was four years into a war it could not finish against a country it could not occupy. The Nanjing massacre in the winter of 1937 to 1938, in which the Japanese army killed civilians and prisoners on a scale still disputed but numbering in the many tens of thousands at minimum, set the character of that occupation. Chinese casualties across the whole conflict ran into the many millions, and Chinese resistance tied down the bulk of the Japanese army for its entire duration — a contribution routinely underweighted in Western accounts. The immediate cause of war with the United States was oil. Japan imported most of it, largely from America, and after Japanese forces moved into southern Indochina in July 1941 the United States, Britain and the Netherlands imposed an embargo. Japan then faced a choice between withdrawing from China, which its leadership regarded as unthinkable, and seizing the oil of the Dutch East Indies, which meant war with the United States. It chose war, and opened it on 7 December 1941 with a carrier strike on the American Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, alongside simultaneous attacks on the Philippines, Malaya and Hong Kong. The raid sank battleships and killed some 2,400 people. It missed the American aircraft carriers, which were at sea, and left the base's fuel storage and repair facilities intact — and it united an American public that had been deeply divided about entering the war. Six months of Japanese victories followed, and then the balance turned at Midway in June 1942, where American codebreakers had read enough of the Japanese naval cipher to know where the attack was coming. Four Japanese fleet carriers were sunk in a single day, along with their aircrew, and Japan never replaced either. What followed was a grinding advance across the Pacific, taking some islands and bypassing others to leave their garrisons isolated, at Guadalcanal, Tarawa, Saipan, Iwo Jima and Okinawa. The fighting was characterised by a refusal to surrender that made each island cost far more than its size suggested, and by the treatment of Allied prisoners, of whom roughly a quarter died in Japanese captivity against a few per cent in German. By 1945 American submarines had strangled Japanese merchant shipping almost completely and firebombing raids had burned out much of urban Japan — a single night's raid on Tokyo in March 1945 killed around 100,000 people, more than either atomic bomb.
